summary: Specifies routing extensions to carry link state information for GMPLS. It enhances the routing extensions needed for MPLS Traffic Engineering. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4202 defines extra routing information for GMPLS traffic engineering. It lets routers describe packet, time-division, wavelength, and fiber links so path computation can choose suitable resources.

questions: what is an interface switching capability descriptor
subtitle: Routing information for traffic-engineered links that may carry packets, time slots, wavelengths or fibers.

tldr.problem: Traditional traffic engineering describes links that have ordinary packet-routing adjacencies. GMPLS also uses optical and time-division links that may not carry routing packets and need different link properties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC generalizes the traffic-engineered link and defines information for unnumbered links, protection, shared failure risks, and interface switching capabilities.
tldr.outcome: It specifies which link-state information GMPLS path computation needs. Separate companion documents define its encoding in OSPF and IS-IS, and RFC 4202 has been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074.

facts.label: Unnumbered link identifier
facts.value: Non-zero 32-bit number, unique within its LSR

facts.label: Shared Risk Link Group identifier
facts.value: 32-bit number, unique within an IGP domain

facts.label: Default interface capability
facts.value: PSC-1 when no descriptor is present

today: RFC 4202 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074. The metadata does not list a document that obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Generalized Traffic-Engineered Link
sections.content:
In traditional traffic engineering, a TE link is associated with an ordinary routing link. Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) also uses resources that cannot send and receive packet by packet, such as optical links, and can represent an LSP or a group of links as one TE link.

RFC 4202 therefore treats a TE link as a logical description of physical resources and their properties. Routers use this information for constrained path computation and GMPLS signaling. Both ends must group the resources consistently, and the link must have a way for its advertising router to determine that it is up.
sections.plainLanguage: A TE link describes resources that a path may use, even when those resources are not ordinary packet links. Routers use the description to choose paths that meet requirements.

sections.title: Describing Different Transport Layers
sections.content:
Transport links may need to carry a particular service, not just provide a requested amount of bandwidth. Path computation may need to account for the supported adaptation, relationships between layers, properties inherited from a lower layer, new layers, and differences among switches.

RFC 4202 sets out principles for layer-specific traffic-engineering attributes, including separating attributes by layer and making their scope clear. This document defines general attributes for a single layer; it leaves inter-layer relationships to future work.
sections.plainLanguage: A path needs links with the right kind of switching and service, not merely enough capacity. The RFC defines single-layer information and leaves relationships between layers out of scope.

sections.title: Keeping Data Traffic off Control Channels
sections.content:
GMPLS control channels carry administrative and signaling traffic, but they may also appear as links in routing. If edge routers send user data over a control channel, its capacity can be exhausted.

One described method checks the interface used to resolve a BGP next hop. If the link-state database says that interface cannot switch packets, the router installs a discard route for the BGP destination. Another option is to keep the GMPLS control-plane address space separate and not advertise control channels into the data network. The RFC notes that other techniques may also be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A control channel carries routing and management messages. Routers can keep user packets off it by rejecting routes that resolve through a non-packet link.

sections.title: Link Identifiers, Protection and Shared Risks
sections.content:
An unnumbered link is point-to-point. Each Label Switching Router assigns it a non-zero 32-bit identifier, unique within that router; advertisements carry the local and remote identifiers. If the remote identifier is unknown, the router uses 0.

The optional Link Protection Type describes the link's protection capability. Shared Risk Link Group information identifies links that share a resource whose failure could affect them all, such as fibers in the same conduit. Path computation can use these properties when it needs protected or diverse paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can identify an unnumbered link without assigning it an IP address. They can also advertise its protection and whether it shares failure risks with other links.

sections.title: Interface Switching Capabilities
sections.content:
The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor states what an interface can switch and which encoding it supports. RFC 4202 defines packet-switching capabilities PSC-1 through PSC-4, Layer-2 switching (L2SC), time-division multiplexing (TDM), lambda switching (LSC), and fiber switching (FSC). If there is no descriptor, the interface is assumed to be PSC-1.

The descriptor can also report properties such as bandwidth limits and MTU, depending on the capability. An interface may advertise multiple descriptors when it supports more than one switching capability. The switching capabilities at opposite ends of a bidirectional link may differ, and the pair of capabilities affects what a label represents.
sections.plainLanguage: The descriptor tells a path planner what each interface can switch. Different links use labels for different resources, such as packets, time slots, wavelengths, or ports.

sections.title: Examples Across Packet and Optical Equipment
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples of descriptors for packet, time-division, and optical equipment. A Gigabit Ethernet packet interface is described as PSC-1. A digital cross-connect can advertise TDM with a supported SDH hierarchy. An optical cross-connect that switches individual wavelengths is described as LSC.

Where a transparent optical cross-connect has no external dense-wavelength-division multiplexing system and does not restrict a port to one wavelength, the interface is described as FSC. A device combining switching functions can advertise multiple descriptors for the same interface, such as one LSC descriptor and one TDM descriptor.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet router, time-division switch, and optical cross-connect advertise different capabilities. A device that supports more than one kind can describe each capability separately.

sections.title: Protecting Routing Information
sections.content:
These extensions may be used to control transport infrastructure, so the information must be transferred using secure or authenticated means. RFC 4202 does not specify how OSPF or IS-IS carries the extensions.

The companion OSPF and IS-IS extension specifications must describe how that information is secured. The routing data should be protected against changes by parties that are not authorized to provide it.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS routing information can affect how transport resources are used. The protocols that carry it must explain how they protect or authenticate it.
